accuracy.evidence: Reflects the research on imitation in early childhood: toddlers learn actions by watching a model and reproducing the steps in order (Meltzoff), and attention to the model is needed before copying. Asking to see a step again is a sensible help-seeking strategy for this age, and the lab never claims copying is the only way to learn.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips toddlers really make: starting to copy before the model has finished, copying only one part instead of the whole sequence, getting the order wrong, looking away at a distraction, and giving up after missing a step. The adult text calls these common mistakes and tells parents how to respond.

lab_distinct.evidence: A learning-to-learn lab with Owl as the model: copying a dance by watching then tapping moves, stacking cups in Owl's colour order, keeping eyes on Owl while a butterfly flies past, slowing down a five-step hand-washing routine, and finally letting Chick copy the child. No other lab uses this watch-then-copy design; it passed the shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step adds one habit of good copying: watch to the end, keep the same order, keep your eyes on the helper, ask to see it again when a step is missed, and become the model yourself. The child tries first and the feedback names which habit made it work.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting options: 'When should you start copying Owl?' (many toddlers say right away), 'Can you copy Owl if your eyes are on the butterfly?' and 'You forgot a step. What is a good thing to do?' with Stop trying as a choice. Each is tested in the lab and the reveal refers back to the choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with tag-specific messages such as 'Watch first. If you grab right away, you miss how Gran does it', 'Same moves, same order. Owl clapped first, so you clap first' and 'Missing a bit is OK. Ask to see it again and keep going.' Each wrong idea gets its own fix.

readability.evidence: Kid text is short and concrete for two and three year olds and passes the family FK gate. Every move button pairs an emoji with one word (clap, stomp, wave, hands up), so a pre-reader can follow while a parent reads the prompt aloud.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no filler words; every sentence teaches a copying habit or gives a parent tip. Explanation duplication is below 12% and the kid explanation keeps to four paragraphs, with nothing restating the title or praising without reason.

mobile.evidence: Walk passed on iPhone 13 and desktop with six steps, five tasks and the challenge completed, each Show me reaching the tick within 6 seconds. Move tiles are large and the butterfly animation stays inside the panel after the centring fix.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported no violations in light or dark theme. The canvas has an aria-label and a live caption naming Owl's current move and step number; all moves are buttons, and the step dots are numbered so nothing depends on colour or motion alone.
